claims.text: At approximately 600°C, simultaneous sliding wear and exposure to an oxygenated corrosive environment accelerate degradation of the eutectic high-entropy alloy.
Mechanical wear repeatedly strips away a protective oxide film during simultaneous wear and corrosion.
Removal of the protective oxide exposes a fresh, reactive alloy surface.
The newly exposed surface rapidly forms a transient, porous, non-protective oxide.
Repeated oxide removal and reformation synergistically enhance both mechanical wear and corrosion.
A multi-phase alloy similar to AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 can possess a native, adherent, protective oxide after prior high-temperature exposure.
The integrity and stability of the near-surface oxide film mediate the alloy's coupled wear–corrosion response.
The reformed porous oxide is less adherent and less protective than the initial oxide.
Loss of the protective oxide increases wear by reducing lubricity and promoting structural damage.
Exposure of fresh reactive alloy increases corrosion through enhanced anodic dissolution.
The simultaneous wear–corrosion condition will produce greater total degradation than either isolated wear or isolated corrosion.
The coupled condition will produce deeper wear tracks than the isolated baseline conditions.
The coupled condition will produce increased mass loss or corrosion current relative to the isolated baseline conditions.
The coupled condition will exhibit a frequently disrupted oxide film.
Wear-only testing in an inert environment will produce moderate wear while leaving the oxide largely intact.
Static corrosion-only testing will produce slower degradation because the oxide film remains stable.
The proposed mechanism requires high temperature, an oxygenated corrosive atmosphere, and sliding wear.
The mechanism may not operate at lower temperatures or without species capable of rapidly reforming a transient non-protective oxide.
